::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** 40 minutes, at home (in class only if there is time: this is early in the cut order).
- **You need:** the `ltee-project` after [lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd); about 3 GB free disk space for the Conda copy of the environment (deleted at the end).
- **You will have:** a Conda environment file for people who do not use Pixi, in your project's `envs/` folder.
:::

## Overview

[Conda](https://docs.conda.io/) (and its faster drop-in, Mamba) is the tool
most bioinformaticians learned first, and the NBIS course this workshop builds
on still teaches it first. Pixi installs **the same packages from the same
channels** (conda-forge, bioconda); what differs is the workflow around them.
You will meet Conda in papers, in lab servers and inside workflow managers, so
you need to read both and convert between them.

This page tries to be fair: Pixi is our main tool because of its lock files
and tasks, not because Conda is bad.

### Learning outcomes

After this page you can:

1. **Translate** everyday Conda commands into Pixi commands and back.
2. **Convert** an existing `environment.yml` into a Pixi workspace.
3. **Export** a Pixi environment so that a Conda or Mamba user can build it, and **build** it.
4. **Explain** what an environment file, an explicit spec and a lock file each guarantee.

## The command table

| What you want | Conda / Mamba | Pixi |
|---------------|---------------|------|
| New environment | `conda create -n ltee -c conda-forge -c bioconda samtools` | `pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda` then `pixi add samtools` |
| Add a package | `conda install -n ltee bwa` | `pixi add bwa` |
| Remove a package | `conda remove -n ltee bwa` | `pixi remove bwa` |
| Use the environment | `conda activate ltee` | `pixi shell` |
| Run one command | `conda run -n ltee samtools --version` | `pixi run samtools --version` |
| See what is installed | `conda list -n ltee` | `pixi list` |
| Share the environment | `conda env export --from-history > environment.yml` | commit `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` |
| Exact versions | `conda list --explicit > spec.txt` (one platform), or the separate `conda-lock` tool | `pixi.lock`, automatic, every platform |
| Rebuild it elsewhere | `conda env create -f environment.yml` | `pixi install --locked` |
| Update | `conda update -n ltee --all` | `pixi update` (within limits) or `pixi upgrade` (raise limits) |
| Delete it | `conda env remove -n ltee` | `pixi clean` (or delete `.pixi/`) |
| Where it lives | one central folder for all environments (`~/miniforge3/envs/`) | inside the project (`.pixi/envs/`) |
| Named commands | not built in (use a Makefile or scripts) | `[tasks]` and `pixi run TASK` |

## 1. From `environment.yml` to Pixi

A labmate sends you the environment file they used for a variant-calling
analysis. Make a folder for this page and save the file there:

```{.bash .run}
mkdir -p ~/cbio7501/conda-comparison
cd ~/cbio7501/conda-comparison
```

```{.yaml filename="environment.yml" .write}
name: variant-calling
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - bioconda
dependencies:
  - python=3.13
  - samtools=1.24
  - bcftools=1.24
```

Turn it into a Pixi workspace and run a tool from it:

```{.bash .run}
pixi init --import environment.yml from-conda
cd from-conda
cat pixi.toml
pixi run bcftools --version | head -1
```

```toml
[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
name = "variant-calling"
platforms = ["osx-arm64"]
version = "0.1.0"

[tasks]

[dependencies]
python = "3.13.*"
samtools = "1.24.*"
bcftools = "1.24.*"
```

Pixi kept the channels and versions (`samtools=1.24` in Conda means
`1.24.*`) and created a lock file. Add your other platforms with
`pixi workspace platform add linux-64 ...` before you share it.

## 2. From Pixi to Conda: an environment file

Now the other direction: a collaborator uses Conda and wants to run your LTEE
pipeline. Export the `pipeline` environment into your project's `envs/`
folder (the template made it for this):

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
pixi workspace export conda-environment -e pipeline envs/pipeline.yml
cat envs/pipeline.yml
```

```yaml
name: pipeline
channels:
- conda-forge
- bioconda
- nodefaults
dependencies:
- fastqc >=0.13.0,<0.14
- multiqc >=1.35,<2
- bwa >=0.7.19,<0.8
- samtools >=1.24,<2
- bcftools >=1.24,<2
- python 3.13.*
- quarto >=1.9
...
```

Notice what it contains: the **ranges** from `pixi.toml`, not the exact
versions from `pixi.lock`. A Conda user who builds it next year may get newer
versions within those ranges.

Build it the way a Conda user would. We use
[micromamba](https://mamba.readthedocs.io/) (a small, standalone Mamba) through
`pixi exec`, so you do not have to install Conda; with Conda the command is
`conda env create -p ./conda-env -f envs/pipeline.yml`. This takes a few
minutes and about 2.5 GB:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec micromamba create -y -p ./conda-env -f envs/pipeline.yml
pixi exec micromamba run -p ./conda-env samtools --version | head -1
pixi exec micromamba run -p ./conda-env fastqc --version
```

```text
samtools 1.24
FastQC v0.13.0
```

::: {.callout-note}
With Conda, tools only work inside the activated environment: FastQC needs
the environment's Java. Calling `./conda-env/bin/fastqc` directly fails with
"Unable to locate a Java Runtime" on macOS. `micromamba run` (like `conda run`
or `conda activate`) sets the environment up first, as `pixi run` does.
:::

## 3. Exact versions for Conda users: explicit specs

To give a Conda user the *exact* packages, export **explicit specs** from the
lock file. There is one file per platform, each a plain list of package URLs
with checksums:

```{.bash .run}
pixi workspace export conda-explicit-spec -e pipeline envs/explicit
ls envs/explicit
head -4 envs/explicit/pipeline_linux-64_conda_spec.txt
```

```text
pipeline_linux-64_conda_spec.txt  pipeline_osx-64_conda_spec.txt  pipeline_osx-arm64_conda_spec.txt
# Generated by `pixi workspace export`
# platform: linux-64
@EXPLICIT
https://conda.anaconda.org/conda-forge/linux-64/libgomp-16.2.0-he0feb66_7.conda#d904c7ddd95e026254b4b80808ee9e12
```

A Conda user builds the exact environment with
`conda create -p ./env --file envs/explicit/pipeline_linux-64_conda_spec.txt`.
This is what the NBIS course does for its students.

## Break it: the right file for the wrong computer

Explicit specs are per platform, and nothing stops you from using the wrong
one. Build an environment from the spec of a platform that is **not** yours:

```{.bash .run}
if [ "$(uname)" = "Darwin" ]; then other=linux-64; else other=osx-arm64; fi
echo "this computer is $(uname), using the spec for $other"
pixi exec micromamba create -y -p ./wrong-env -f envs/explicit/pipeline_${other}_conda_spec.txt
```

It "works": the packages download and install without a single warning. Now
use it:

```{.bash .expect-fail}
pixi exec micromamba run -p ./wrong-env samtools --version
```

```text
.../wrong-env/bin/samtools: cannot execute binary file
```

The programs were built for another operating system. `pixi.lock` cannot be
used this way by mistake: it holds all platforms, and Pixi picks the one that
matches your computer. Clean up both Conda copies (5 GB):

```{.bash .run}
rm -rf ./conda-env ./wrong-env
```

## What each file guarantees

| File | Who writes it | Pins | Platforms |
|------|---------------|------|-----------|
| `environment.yml` (hand-written or `--from-history`) | you | what you asked for, often loosely | any (solved again on each machine) |
| `conda env export` without `--from-history` | Conda | exact versions **and builds** of one machine | only that platform; often fails elsewhere |
| explicit spec (`--explicit`) | Conda or Pixi | exact files and checksums | one file per platform |
| `pixi.lock` | Pixi | exact files and checksums | every platform in the manifest, in one file |

None of them pins the hardware, the operating system's own libraries, the
data, or that the channels will still serve the packages in ten years
([lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd#prove-it-rebuild-from-the-lock-file)).

## Where Conda is still a good choice

- **Your lab or cluster already runs on it.** Shared Conda environments on a
  server, or HPC modules built with Conda, are fine to keep using.
- **Workflow managers speak Conda.** Snakemake's `conda:` directive and
  Nextflow's `conda` profile take `environment.yml` files; nf-core pipelines
  ship them. The export in step 2 is how you connect a Pixi project to them
  ([lesson 09](09-snakemake.qmd), [lesson 10](10-nextflow.qmd)).
- **One quick, throwaway environment** for trying a tool: either works
  (`pixi exec` is the Pixi way).
- **Lock files exist for Conda too**, through [conda-lock](https://conda.github.io/conda-lock/).

And Pixi's honest downsides: it is young and still changes often (version
0.x; commands are renamed now and then), each project has its own copy of its
environment (our pipeline environment is 2.4 GB; the shared package cache
avoids downloading twice), and fewer tutorials and Stack Overflow answers
exist than for Conda.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `pixi init --import` fails on `pip:` entries | Pixi imports Conda packages; add PyPI packages afterwards with `pixi add --pypi NAME`. |
| A Conda colleague's `environment.yml` has build strings (`samtools=1.24=h36b3a25_2`) | It came from `conda env export` on one platform. Remove the build strings (the part after the second `=`) before importing. |
| `micromamba: command not found` | Run it through Pixi as shown: `pixi exec micromamba ...`. |
| Disk full after this page | `rm -rf ./conda-env ./wrong-env`, and `pixi exec micromamba clean --all -y` to empty micromamba's cache. |

## Apply it to your own mini-analysis

Export your capstone's environment with `pixi workspace export
conda-environment` into `envs/`, and mention in your README that Conda users
can build it from there.

## Key points

- Pixi and Conda use the same packages and channels; Pixi adds per-project environments, automatic lock files for all platforms, and tasks.
- `pixi init --import environment.yml` converts a Conda environment; `pixi workspace export` goes the other way.
- An exported `environment.yml` carries ranges; explicit specs carry exact packages for one platform; `pixi.lock` carries exact packages for all platforms.
- Conda is still fine for shared servers and workflow-manager integrations.
